en: The Ritual for Inviting Piṇḍola,
translated by the Song Dynasty śramaṇa Shi Huijian.
In the kingdom of India, there were upāsakas, kings, elders, and householders who, whenever they established a universal assembly, would always...
He invited the Arhat Piṇḍola Bharadvāja.

"Piṇḍola" is his personal name, and "Bharadvāja" is his clan name. Because he manifested supernatural powers for the sake of the elder Jyotiṣka, the Buddha expelled him and did not permit him to enter parinirvāṇa, commanding that he serve as a field of merit for the fourfold assembly during the age of the final Dharma.
Whenever you wish to do so, burn incense and prostrate yourself in a quiet place, facing toward Mount Malaya in India; with a sincere heart, invoke his name, saying:
"Virtuous Pindola Bharadvaja, you who have received the Buddha’s command to serve as a field of merit for those in the age of the Dharma's decline."
"I pray that you accept my invitation to eat here.
If one has newly constructed a dwelling, one should likewise invite him, saying:
"I pray that you accept my invitation to stay and sleep here in this house upon the bedding provided."
If the entire community of monks is invited for a communal bath, one should likewise invite him, saying:
"I pray that you accept my invitation to bathe here.

Before dawn, one should prepare fragrant decoctions, pure water, bathing powder, and willow twigs; the oil should be blended with water to a temperature suitable for bathing. Following the method of human bathing, one should open the door and invite him inside, then close the door. After a short while, as if he has finished his bath, the community of monks may enter.

Whenever there is a communal meal or a ritual bathing, it is essential that all invite the Sangha; only when one seeks liberation with a mind free from doubt or delusion and possesses pure faith may they be requested to attend.

In recent times, there was an elder who heard it said that the Arhat Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, having received the Buddha’s command, acts as a field of merit for those in the age of the Dharma's decline. He immediately prepared a great assembly according to the Dharma and with a sincere heart invited Piṇḍola, spreading flowers beneath the woolen rug, wishing thereby to verify [the truth].
When the great assembly had finished eating, the *kūrpa* rugs and flowers all withered. Distressed and self-reproaching, they did not know from where this fault originated.
They again exhausted their efforts in questioning the scripture masters and once more convened a great assembly; yet, as before, the flowers all withered once again.
Furthermore, he exhausted his family’s entire wealth and property to convene another great assembly; yet, as before, he was filled with remorse and reproached himself.
He again invited over a hundred Dharma masters to seek the recovery of what was lost and to repent for his transgressions.
For instance, there was once an elder who, being advanced in years, went forth in the four directions to repent for his transgressions.
The elder addressed him, saying:
"You invited me to three assemblies, and I accepted every invitation."
"When you yourself sent a slave to block me at the gate, he thought that because I was old and my clothes were tattered, I had been expelled.

The ascetic Rādha would not allow me to come forward; when I attempted to force my way in at your request, your slave struck me on the head with a staff, breaking it and causing a wound on the right side of my forehead."
The second assembly also came, yet I did not see the previous one.
I again wished to force my way in, but they struck me once more, wounding the center of my forehead.
The third assembly also came; as before, I was beaten, suffering a wound on the left corner of my forehead.
"All this was done by you yourself; why do you lament?
Having said this, he vanished. The elder then realized it was Piṇḍola.
From that time forward, when people made offerings of merit, none dared to block their gates again.
If Piṇḍola arrives, the flowers upon his seat will not wither.

When one has newly constructed a dwelling or prepared a bed and wishes to invite Piṇḍola, one should always sprinkle the ground with fragrant water and light lamps of scented oil. One should spread new beds and new mattresses with cotton batting, and cover the cotton with white silk cloth.
At the beginning of the night, invite him according to the Dharma; then, close the door of the room and be careful not to look inside with negligence or disrespect.
Each person should, with a sincere heart, believe that he will certainly come; when such refined sincerity moves Heaven and Earth, there is nothing that it cannot reach.
When he arrived, he appeared as a monastic in the upper quarters where there was a place for reclining; he also appeared in the bathhouse using hot water.

When receiving invitations to great assemblies, he would appear either in the seat of honor, in the middle seat, or in a lower seat, manifesting himself in the form of a monk according to the circumstances; though people sought to distinguish him from others, they could never find any difference.
After he had departed, [the Buddha] saw that the flowers where he had sat had not withered, and thus he knew it was him.
He then requested the dharma for inviting Piṇḍola.
